summary: For ages 12–14, pupils evaluate the sustainable use of finite raw materials (metals, minerals, fossil fuels). The core assessed skill is EVALUATION: weighing the energy and resource savings of recycling against its own costs to reach a justified judgement, rather than reciting that recycling is 'good'. Pupils should see why resources are finite (formation over geological timescales versus consumption over years), name a concrete environmental cost of extraction (land damage and tailings from mining, energy and CO2 from smelting), and understand recycling as a quantitative trade-off anchored by the illustrative figure that recycling aluminium uses roughly 5% of the energy of primary extraction. They should also frame the circular economy — reduce, reuse, recycle — as keeping materials in use, contrasted with a linear take–make–dispose path.
misconceptions: Thinking finite resources will 'never run out' because reserves seem huge, ignoring the mismatch between formation and consumption rates.
Believing recycling is free or cost-free good, overlooking its energy, collection and sorting costs.
Assuming all materials recycle equally well and indefinitely, ignoring quality loss and contamination limits.
Confusing renewable energy resources with the finite mineral/metal resources this topic centres on.
Treating 'recycling is good' as the answer rather than evaluating the trade-off for a specific case.

activities.title: Steer a resource system over time
steps: Start with a finite ore stock and a city that consumes a fixed amount of metal each year; let the years tick and watch the ore stock bar drain while an energy dial and a CO2 counter climb.

Increase the recycling-rate control and observe how it changes new-ore demand and energy use. In a model with constant material demand, no losses and complete recovery, ore extraction may stop; with incomplete recovery or growing demand it usually continues more slowly. Use the roughly 5% aluminium energy figure as an illustrative comparison, not a guarantee for every material or process.

Read the looping material as a circular economy — reduce, reuse, recycle keeps materials in use — and contrast it with a linear take–make–dispose line where each product ends as waste and new ore must be mined.
As you raise recycling further, watch a collection-and-sorting cost meter rise, so 'just recycle everything' meets a genuine trade-off.

Tune the consumption and recycling controls to slow ore depletion as much as you can justify (with incomplete recovery the finite stock still drains slowly, so a truly steady state needs reduced use or near-complete recovery), then write down where you set each control and justify the balance you chose between energy saved and recycling's own cost.
activities.insight: Choices about consumption and recycling drive resource stocks, energy use and emissions over time; a circular economy that keeps materials in use can save substantial energy (large for aluminium; the amount varies by material) and slows depletion of finite ore compared with a linear take–make–dispose path, but recycling carries its own collection/sorting costs, so the best policy is a justified balance, not an absolute.

activities.title: Defend a recycling decision
steps: Take on the role of someone arguing for or against a specific recycling scheme (e.g. kerbside aluminium collection for a town).
State your judgement and give at least two reasons, naming both a benefit (energy saved, ore conserved) and a cost (collection, sorting, transport, quality loss).
Respond when challenged with a counter-cost or counter-benefit, revising or defending your position with reasons.
activities.insight: A sound evaluation names the trade-offs on both sides and reaches a justified conclusion for a specific case, rather than asserting recycling is automatically right.

activities.title: Explore the life cycle of a material
steps: Work through an illustrated life-cycle scene — ore → mine → smelt → product → recycle → back to product — revealing the impact and energy fact at each stage.
Sort example resources into finite (metal ores, fossil fuels, minerals) versus genuinely renewable, and say what makes each finite one finite.
Match each extraction activity (mining, smelting, fossil-fuel burning) to its environmental impact (waste rock/tailings and land damage; high energy use and CO2; greenhouse-gas emissions).
State, for aluminium, roughly what fraction of extraction energy recycling uses, and explain which expensive step (electrolysis from ore) recycling avoids.
Describe how the recycle stage closes the loop into a circular economy (reduce, reuse, recycle) instead of a linear take–make–dispose path.
activities.insight: Builds the vocabulary and factual grounding — which resources are finite and why, the specific impacts of extraction, where the energy cost sits, and how a circular economy keeps materials in use — that the evaluation then draws on.

checkQuestion: When you throw an aluminium can in the bin, a student says 'the metal gets used up and destroyed, so we just have to keep mining more — that's why recycling doesn't really matter.' Is the metal destroyed when we use it? Then the important part: explain why recycling a metal saves so much compared with getting new metal from its ore.
checkAnswer: The metal isn't destroyed — the aluminium atoms still exist, just dispersed in landfill; that's why it CAN be recycled. Recycling saves because extracting new aluminium from its ore needs huge energy (electrolysis) plus mining, transport and land damage, whereas melting collected cans uses a small fraction of that energy and avoids new mining. Full marks reject 'destroyed' AND ground the saving in the energy/impact of extraction vs re-melting.
